bridge: From L01, create a folder, change into it and inspect a text file. From P06, recognise why .venv is generated setup rather than authored source. Check git --version; if Git is absent, install it from git-scm.com using your system’s documented route. This is a local exercise; no GitHub account or upload is needed.
teaching:
Think of three places for your work: the editable desk, a tray of changes selected for saving, and the recorded history. Git calls these the working tree, staging area and commits. Editing a note changes the desk. git add note.txt copies its current content into the tray. git commit records what is in the tray. Later edits do not secretly update the recorded snapshot.

Git stores snapshots connected by history. The working tree is what you edit. The index, also called staging, selects content for the next commit. A commit records the staged snapshot, author information and a message. Saving a file in an editor does not stage it, and staging does not create a commit.

Use status and diff before each commit. Stage explicit paths so unrelated notes, environment folders or secrets are not swept into history. A later deletion does not remove a secret from earlier commits. If you ever expose a real secret, revocation and a deliberate history cleanup are separate tasks.

Branches are names pointing to commits. A merge combines histories and may need human conflict resolution. In this course, use a local disposable repository to learn conflicts; do not rewrite a reviewed team's history as a shortcut. A lab notebook should record why a change was made and how it was verified, not only the command list.

Read working tree, index and HEAD as three different states. git add stages the file content as it exists then; later edits are not automatically added. git diff compares tracked working content with the index; git diff --cached compares the index with HEAD; git diff HEAD shows tracked working changes relative to HEAD. git status also identifies untracked files that a normal diff does not include. git commit -a does not add new untracked files.

The course video uses master as its branch name; a repository may instead use main or another configured name. A branch is a movable reference, while a commit object is identified by its content. Do not use a content hash as proof of trusted authorship. Existing snapshots can retain deleted working files, so deleting a large working file does not remove it from repository history. A clean textual merge can still combine incompatible behaviours; verify the intended result. The selected Cyber excerpt includes a complete two-branch conflict and resolution; it excludes forced checkout. For shared review work use explicit fetch/merge according to project policy. git pull can integrate using different configured strategies, so do not assume every pull is a merge or rewrite a shared branch without authorisation.

For this disposable repository, configure a local practice author after git init: git config user.name "Practice Learner" and git config user.email "learner@example.invalid". Omit --global so you do not alter other repositories. The address is a fictional example, not a delivery destination. Use git status after every operation; it tells you what is staged, modified or untracked. If a commit fails, read its error before repeating commands; failure does not by itself delete your file.
example:
mkdir git-lab
cd git-lab
git init
printf 'first version\n' > note.txt
git status --short
git add note.txt
git diff --cached
git commit -m 'docs: Add practice note'
printf 'second version\n' > note.txt
git diff
# Requires a locally configured Git author identity.
explanation: Before staging, note.txt is untracked. After git add, its exact contents are in the index. The commit captures first version. The later edit appears in git diff but not in that existing commit. If author identity is missing, follow Git's setup documentation; the failure does not mean the file disappeared.
exercise: Perform the shown local history. Stage the second version, inspect the staged diff and commit it. Use git log --oneline and git show to find the two versions. Record each commit's purpose in a separate nonsecret lab log.
solution: Two commits show first version followed by second version. A clean status after the second commit means no current unstaged/staged edits, not that the history lacks sensitive material.
challenge: In the disposable repository, first run git status and finish or save any uncommitted practice edits. Create a branch with git switch -c left, replace the note’s single line with left, then add and commit note.txt. Create another branch from the previous commit with git switch -c right HEAD~1, replace that same line with right, then add and commit it. While on right, run git merge left. Inspect the conflict, choose a deliberate final sentence, remove the marker lines, stage note.txt and commit. Explain why Git could not choose the sentence for you. This exercise stays local.
challenge_solution: Both branches changed the same original line in different ways, so a conflict is expected. The file contains marker lines separating left and right alternatives. After choosing a sentence, verify the file has no marker lines and contains the intended text, then run git add note.txt and git commit with a message explaining the resolution. git log --graph --oneline shows a merge with two parents. A successful merge command alone is not enough: reread the final note. HEAD~1 in the supplied sequence means the commit immediately before the left-branch edit; confirm this history before using it elsewhere.
